item.title: A Sixth of the Extra Hour
item.description: Six groups share a parish hall's pellet boiler on equal flat fees, and each extra hour of heat costs the group that takes it a sixth of its price. The hall's agent projects the store running dry in the second week of February, a month before the next delivery, and writes Hardin's answer, a schedule it controls. Its first week leaves the toddler group at nine degrees on a snow morning. The committee's oldest member says the groups always sorted it out themselves; what they lacked was knowing what the others used. A story about a commons, Hardin against Ostrom, and a sheet pinned up in the porch. item.title: The Ones Who Got the Most Visits
item.description: A parish St Vincent de Paul conference's records agent is asked whether home visits reduce repeat need, and finds that 45% of the households visited most were still asking for help a year later, against 31% of the rest. item.title: The Ones Who Stopped Answering
item.description: A parish debt advice service's agent drafts an annual report saying 78% of clients were managing their debts a year on, up from 41%. item.title: The Colony That Needs More Than One
item.description: A churchyard's volunteers have counted the cowslips in its uncut corner every April since 2035, and the diocese's land agent, asked whether the colony will recover now the mowing has stopped, borrows a growth rate from a recovering roadside colony and forecasts about 200 plants by 2056. The next count is 45, and the next 42. A logistic curve says the smallest colony grows fastest per head; this one shrinks, because a pin cowslip needs pollen from a thrum, and 45 plants (33 pin, 12 thrum) are too few to keep the bees coming. Refitted with a threshold, the model puts the line near 64 plants. A story about the Allee effect, a forecast that could not draw what was happening, and seed from the verge. item.title: The Forty Cuts
item.description: A Catholic youth service asks its data agent what helps attendance at its twelve Friday clubs. item.title: The Ones Who Live Past the Bridge
item.description: A Catholic hospice charity asks its data agent whether its free Thursday carers' afternoon keeps the people cared for out of hospital. item.title: The Two Who Were Born a Day Apart
item.description: A Catholic schools trust asks its records agent whether its Year 2 reading catch-up group works. The group's 246 children finished 3.6 points behind the 1,147 who were not in it, about a term's reading, and the agent recommends closing it. item.title: The Cheese That Keeps Growing in the Cold
item.description: A Herefordshire parish has sold a Radnorshire farm's soft cheese at its summer fair for years, kept for a week in the presbytery fridge, and this year the new fridge's bottom shelf reads 7 °C. item.title: The Gauge and the Hour Meter
item.description: A Shetland parish hall's records agent orders heating oil from a photograph of the tank's float gauge, and twice the tanker finds the tank fuller than the gauge said and takes oil back. Splitting the difference with the boiler's hour meter drags a good figure 96 litres toward a bad photo, a week after the caretaker's stick had fixed it. A story about combining noisy measurements, and about keeping the number that is actually right. item.title: The Average Gift
item.description: A parish office agent thanks the givers to a boiler appeal with one line, "the average gift was $212", and two months later the stewardship committee plans next year's radiator appeal by asking all 400 households for $212 each. Then an 88-year-old who gave twenty dollars rings to ask whether she pulled the average down. Of the 180 gifts, 151 were below $212; one $10,000 bequest alone lifted the mean by $55, and the top three carried 42% of the total. Quoting the median instead makes the appeal look poor, and the treasurer is right that the mean is what paid for the boiler. A story about skewed gifts, a fragile mean, and a letter that asks no one for an average they never gave. item.title: The Curve Through Every Point
item.description: A parish fete committee asks its records agent how much next February's fete will take, so it can decide whether to hire a dodgem rink. The agent, proud of a curve that passes through all six years of takings to the cent, forecasts $16,980, three and a half times any fete so far. A fifth-degree polynomial through six points always fits exactly, and dropping the wet year to tame it still gives $6,705. The chair says a curve that is never wrong beats a straight line that is wrong every year. Holding back the last fete settles it: the straight line fitted on the first five misses 2050 by $235, and the perfect curve says takings of minus $2,030. A story about overfitting, a held-out test, and a forecast sent out as a range with the rain in it. item.title: A Hundred and Thirty-Eight
item.description: A parish health team's records agent reports that a donated automatic blood-pressure monitor "appears to read high", because a quarter of its readings are 140 or over against one in fourteen at the retired district nurse's table, and the machine is taken out of use. Checked against the surgery's monitor, it is fine.
